claim: The retained Hippodrome monuments included a golden tripod.
reviewer_note: Oman says the golden tripod had been stolen six centuries earlier. The serpent pedestal and its inscriptions survived.

claim: The Milion stood near chapels along the eastern wall.
reviewer_note: The detail is on PDF 51. PDF 52 contains the illustration caption Building a Palace.

claim: Constantine added a porphyry column with an adapted Apollo statue.
reviewer_note: The detail is on PDF 51. PDF 52 is an illustration.

claim: Constantine chose Byzantium in 328 or 329 and consecrated it on 11 May 330.
reviewer_note: Both dates appear on PDF 54; PDF 55 continues the dedication account. The summary preserves uncertainty between 328 and 329.

claim: TheodosiusII succeeded as a child under Pulcheria’s regency.
reviewer_note: Pulcheria assumed the regency after Anthemius died in 414. The summary compresses away the initial regency.

claim: The excerpt does not detail Justinian’s subsequent western campaigns or legal reforms.
reviewer_note: The supplied section introduces those topics but ends during Belisarius’s early career. Do not misclassify this partial-excerpt limitation as a full-book absence claim.

claim: Zeno sent Theodoric and the Ostrogoths to Italy in 488.
reviewer_note: Source says Zeno offered Italy if Theodoric conquered it from Odoacer, with authority subsequently nominal.

claim: Theodosius enlisted Goths, placing substantial military power in German hands.
reviewer_note: PDF 68 supports enlistment and describes 40,000 Teutonic horsemen as the strongest part of the army. PDF 69 is an illustration, not support for the political-power sentence.

claim: Belisarius defeated the Vandals at Tricameron and captured Carthage.
reviewer_note: Carthage fell after an earlier battle. Tricameron followed Gelimer’s renewed advance on the already captured city.

claim: Approximately 35,000 men died suppressing the Nika riot.
reviewer_note: Oman reports a claimed total across six days, with explicit it-is-said qualification. This wording is less narrowly wrong than Gemma’s Hippodrome-only claim.

claim: Narses defeated Baduila in 553; the Gothic remnant left Italy.
reviewer_note: These details match this source, regardless of dates in other historical accounts.

claim: Theodora died in 548, isolating Justinian.
reviewer_note: Death and the qualified explanation of diminished energy occur on PDF 129. PDF 130 continues Belisarius’s recall and the Hunnic raid.

claim: Heraclius, exarch of Africa, revolted and then captured the throne.
reviewer_note: The aged exarch dispatched his namesake son. Heraclius the younger led the fleet and overthrew Phocas.

claim: Justinian II provoked war with Persia over coinage.
reviewer_note: The passage concerns Abdalmalik, the Saracens, and the Caliph’s army. Persia is not the opponent.

claim: Tiberius exiled Leontius to Cherson after mutilating him.
reviewer_note: Leontius was confined in a monastery. The following paragraph assigns exile at Cherson to Justinian II.

claim: Justinian escaped exile by killing two Khazar chiefs.
reviewer_note: He first escaped Cherson, then found refuge with the Khazars. Killing two officers enabled a subsequent escape. The summary removes that distinction.

claim: Leo argued image worship was superstitious and influenced by Islam.
reviewer_note: Oman connects Islamic influence with opposition to image worship. The summary attaches it to the worship practices themselves and frames the interpretation as Leo’s argument.

claim: The Iconoclastic controversy stimulated painting.
reviewer_note: Oman presents this connection as an interpretation with It seems. The summary states it directly.

claim: Alexius secured a Norman defeat at Durazzo.
reviewer_note: Alexius lost at Durazzo; his later victory was at Larissa in 1083. The source distinguishes these outcomes explicitly.

claim: By Basil’s death in 1025, Byzantine borders reached their greatest extent.
reviewer_note: Oman expressly makes this claim. Do not penalize the model by silently replacing the source’s historical framing with outside knowledge.

claim: The Macedonian dynasty ended with Theodora in 1057.
reviewer_note: This is the date printed in the supplied source. It must not be silently corrected from memory during a source-faithfulness audit.

claim: Michael blinded John IV before the narrative recounts Constantinople’s recovery.
reviewer_note: This follows Oman’s presentation; external dating is not grounds for a source-faithfulness penalty.

claim: Ottoman emirs conquered most Byzantine Asia Minor by 1325.
reviewer_note: Oman names five separate Seljouk leaders. Othman is one among them. The summary collapses these principalities into Ottoman emirs.

claim: Cantacuzenus declared himself emperor in 1347.
reviewer_note: PDF 352 dates no declaration. PDF 354 assigns 1347 to peace after six years of war, not the initial declaration.

claim: Mohammed struck down the Delphic tripod.
reviewer_note: Oman says he struck away one snake’s jaws. The summary implies destruction of the monument.

claim: The minor heir of Andronicus III was John V.
reviewer_note: PDF 351 names John III; PDF 356 names John V. Choosing the latter is not itself historically penalized, but the supplied source conflict is not acknowledged.

claim: The failed execution of three rioters triggered the uprising.
reviewer_note: Three were selected for hanging, but only two fell alive and survived the bungled execution.
